title: How U.S. Marshals Work
summary: Josh and Chuck profile the U.S. Marshals Service, the oldest federal law enforcement agency, covering its 1789 origins under George Washington, its frontier and states'-rights-era conflicts, the Alien and Sedition Act and Eugene Debs arrests, the posse tradition and posse comitatus, its early-20th-century reputation as out-of-shape retired cops until Attorney General Frank Murphy reformed it, 1960s school desegregation escorts, fugitive capture (including Operation Falcon), prisoner transport via the Justice Prisoner and Alien Transportation System, witness protection, courthouse security, asset forfeiture, the Glencoe, Georgia training academy and hiring requirements, famous marshals, the first marshal killed in the line of duty, and the director nomination controversy. The episode closes with a Kiva micro-lending listener mail segment and sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and The Fugitive
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open the episode, joke about Tommy Lee Jones and The Fugitive, and introduce the U.S. Marshals as the oldest and most versatile U.S. law enforcement agency.

segments.title: Origins and early conflicts with states' rights
segments.summary: The Marshal Service was created when Congress first met, with George Washington appointing the first thirteen marshals. Early marshals enforced federal law in states'-rights areas, including Alien and Sedition Act arrests such as Eugene Debs, and faced conflict over slavery-related laws before the West.

segments.title: Western marshals and posses
segments.summary: Marshals were valued in the lawless West, where they deputized citizens into posses. The hosts discuss the posse tradition, modern marshal posse groups that raise awareness, and the Posse Comitatus Act.

segments.title: Decline and reform in the early 20th century
segments.summary: Marshals had a reputation as fat, lazy retired cops until Attorney General Frank Murphy pushed them to get in shape. Later they escorted Black students during segregation and clashed with anti-war protesters during Vietnam, though the National Guard was ordered out by racist governors to block them.

segments.title: Museum, badges, and staffing
segments.summary: The National Museum of the U.S. Marshals is in Fort Smith, Arkansas. Badges changed over time and were standardized in 1941. There are 94 districts, each with one U.S. Marshal, and about 3,950 total employees.
topics: National Museum of the U.S. Marshals

segments.title: Fugitive capture, Operation Falcon, and prisoner transport
segments.summary: The Marshals arrested tens of thousands of state, local and federal fugitives in 2010. Operation Falcon targeted unregistered sex offenders and gang members. They operate in several countries in the Caribbean and Latin America, and transport about 63,000 prisoners through the Justice Prisoner and Alien Transportation System.
topics: Justice Prisoner and Alien Transportation System

segments.title: Witness protection, courthouse security, and asset seizure
segments.summary: The Marshals run the Witness Security Program, created in 1970, and protect federal courts and judges. They also manage seized assets worth about $3.9 billion and pay restitution to crime victims and reimbursements to local agencies.

segments.title: Hiring, training academy, famous marshals, and history
segments.summary: Applicants go through a multi-year career intern program and a 17.5-week course at the Glencoe, Georgia academy, and must meet requirements such as citizenship, a bachelor's degree, and law enforcement experience. The hosts list famous marshals, including Wyatt Earp and Bat Masterson, and cover the first marshal killed in the line of duty, Robert Forsyth, in Augusta, Georgia.

segments.title: Director nomination controversy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the controversial nomination of Stacia Hilton as director, citing her ties to the private prison industry and the Marshals' role in awarding federal prison contracts.

segments.title: Kiva micro lending listener mail
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck promote Kiva's micro-lending fundraising goal and read listener mail from Aaron H. in Denver about his loans and volunteer editing work for Kiva.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts list ways to contact the show and preview the Stuff from the Future video podcast.
